title: A benchmark check asks whether each result lies inside a published interval and how it moves with the mesh; a manufactured-solution check asks whether the error falls at the designed rate
summary: Three panels compare drag, lift and pressure drop for flow past a cylinder in a channel with published reference intervals at two mesh sizes, and two log-log panels give the error of a manufactured three-dimensional Stokes solution at three mesh sizes with measured orders. Read both for what the points can and cannot establish with so few meshes.

media.alt: Three side-by-side panels plotting a measured value at two mesh sizes, 0.05 and 0.035, joined by a blue line, over a green band for a published reference interval. Left: drag coefficient falls from 6.396 to 6.124 and enters the band 6.05 to 6.25. Middle: lift coefficient falls from 0.093 to minus 0.012, crossing a very thin band near 0.008 to 0.01. Right: pressure drop falls from 0.166 to 0.162, the first point inside the band 0.165 to 0.175 and the second just below it.

source.note: The page teaches the generic reading of a benchmark-interval check and of a convergence plot with measured order. The DFG 3D-1Z reference intervals are printed in the figure legends; the orders are printed in the panel titles and reproduced from read-off errors in the Apply script. The cfdcore project holds a convergence figure with its own explainer.

read_the_figure.question: At the mesh sizes tried, does the solver reproduce the published drag, lift and pressure drop for flow past a cylinder, and does the error of a known 3D solution fall at a rate better than a stated bar as the mesh is refined?
read_the_figure.axes: Benchmark: three panels share the x axis, mesh size lc from 0.05 on the left to 0.035 on the right (the axis label says coarse to fine, right to left); y is the coefficient (drag, lift) or the pressure difference, with a green band for the published interval. Manufactured solution: x is mesh size h on a log axis, inverted, y is the L2 error of velocity (left) and pressure (right) on log axes.
look_at: Benchmark: only two meshes; each curve is a single straight line segment, so slope is the only shape it can show.
Drag: the coarse point is above the band at 6.396, the fine point inside it at 6.124.
Lift: the line crosses the thin reference band and goes negative; the values are of the order of the change between meshes, not of the reference.
Pressure drop: the coarse point (0.166) is inside the band; the fine point (0.162) is below it.
Manufactured solution: both error curves are straight on log-log axes; the titles give the orders, 2.92 and 2.97 for velocity, 3.83 and 3.82 for pressure.
Manufactured solution: the third point of each curve touches the lower right corner and is partly hidden by the frame; x tick labels overlap.
read_the_figure.proves: Drag moves into the published interval with refinement. Lift changes sign between two meshes and is not converged. Pressure drop is close to the interval and slightly below it on the fine mesh. The manufactured-solution test shows errors falling at orders close to 3 for velocity and above 3.8 for pressure over three coarse meshes, beating the stated acceptance bars of 2.5 and 1.5.
if_wrong: Drag outside the interval at all meshes and drifting away: the boundary conditions, the reference area or the nondimensionalisation differ from the benchmark.
A lift that changes sign with refinement: the quantity is a small difference of large contributions and needs much finer meshes or a different evaluation.
Orders that fall as the mesh is refined: pre-asymptotic behaviour or an error source that does not scale with h.
An order far above theory: a manufactured solution that the discrete space represents especially well, or a pre-asymptotic range.
must_check: The coefficients are defined as in the benchmark (reference length, area and velocity).
At least three meshes, so that an order or a trend can be fitted and a sign change can be told from noise.
The mesh-size axis is labelled in the direction the data run.
The element pair or scheme is stated so the expected orders are known.
Acceptance bars are compared with the theoretical orders, not set so loosely that anything passes.
as_drawn: Benchmark, drag: 6.396 at lc = 0.05 and 6.124 at lc = 0.035; band 6.05 to 6.25. Banner: PASS, 6.396 to 6.124.
Benchmark, lift: 0.093 at 0.05 and -0.012 at 0.035; band 0.008 to 0.01. Banner: FINDING.
Benchmark, pressure drop: 0.166 at 0.05 and 0.162 at 0.035; band 0.165 to 0.175. Banner: FINDING, 0.166 to 0.162.
Benchmark x axis tick labels run 0.0500 on the left to 0.0350 on the right while the label says coarse to fine, right to left.

Manufactured solution: velocity error about 8e-2, 2.5e-2 and 1.05e-2 (third partly clipped); pressure error steeper; orders [2.92, 2.97] and [3.83, 3.82]; bars > 2.5 and > 1.5; both PASS. Footnote: unit cube, n = (4, 6, 8).

terms.meaning: The force on the body along and across the stream, made dimensionless with a reference dynamic pressure and area defined by the benchmark.
The difference of pressure between two probe points upstream and downstream of the body, in the benchmark's nondimensional units.
A published range for each quantity, obtained from many codes on very fine meshes; a result inside it counts as agreement.
A chosen smooth velocity and pressure field, inserted in the equations to compute the forcing, so the exact error of the solver is known.
The slope of the log error against the log mesh size between two meshes.
The root mean square difference between computed and exact fields over the domain.
Writing the velocity as the curl of a vector field makes it divergence-free by construction, which suits incompressible manufactured solutions.

remember: Two meshes give one slope; a trend or an order needs at least three.
A quantity that is a small difference of large contributions, like lift on a nearly symmetric body, is the last to converge.
A benchmark pass means the setup (definitions, boundary conditions) matches as well as the solver.
An observed order is only meaningful in the asymptotic range, and coarse meshes may be outside it.
State the acceptance bar and why it is set where it is.

understand.title: What a benchmark interval is
understand.text: For the 3D-1Z flow past a cylinder, groups of codes computed drag, lift and pressure drop on very fine meshes and published the spread. Falling inside an interval says your result is within the spread of established codes. It does not say the discretisation has converged, and it says nothing about quantities not in the table.

understand.title: Why lift is hard
understand.text: On a nearly symmetric configuration the lift is a small sum of large positive and negative pressure and shear contributions, so it is sensitive to mesh. Here it moves from 0.093 to -0.012 between two meshes, a change roughly ten times the width of the reference value. A sign change between two meshes means the answer is not yet determined at this resolution.

understand.title: What an observed order verifies
understand.text: If the discrete solution converges to the manufactured one at a rate set by the element, the error follows a power of h. A measured slope near the theoretical value on three meshes supports that the equations, forcing and discretisation are consistent. It cannot detect an error that is smaller than the discretisation error, and coarse meshes may sit before the asymptotic range.

understand.title: Pressure order above velocity order
understand.text: The velocity error converges at about 3 and the pressure at about 3.8. For a common stable pair with velocity of degree k and pressure of degree k - 1 the L2 pressure error is expected to converge at about k - 1 + 1, one order lower than velocity, so a pressure order above the velocity order calls for an explanation: a smooth manufactured pressure, a higher-degree pressure space, or coarse meshes. The element is not stated.

steps.title: Drag coefficient
steps.note: U and A_ref are fixed by the benchmark specification; the figure does not state them, so check them against the benchmark before comparing.

steps.title: Is the result inside the interval
steps.note: For drag the fine-mesh value 6.124 satisfies 6.05 to 6.25; the coarse value 6.396 does not.

steps.title: Where the lift line crosses the band
steps.note: Linear interpolation between two points gives a crossing near lc = 0.038. With two meshes it is a guide to the eye, not a prediction.

steps.title: Observed order
steps.note: With meshes of n = 4, 6, 8 cells per side, h scales as 1/n.

steps.title: Predicting the third point
steps.note: With p of about 2.97 and e_2 of about 2.5e-2, the third velocity error is about 1.1e-2. The figure's third marker lies there.

steps.title: Divergence-free by construction
steps.note: A vector identity. In two dimensions a single stream function does this job; in three dimensions a vector potential replaces it.

worked.title: Order from read-off errors, and the third point
worked.problem: Velocity L2 errors read from the figure are about 0.083 on the coarsest mesh (n = 4) and 0.025 on the middle mesh (n = 6). What order does that give, and what error would you expect on the n = 8 mesh?

solution.text: Observed order between the first two meshes, with h proportional to 1/n.
Predicted error on the third mesh.

worked.answer: About 2.96, matching the printed 2.92 to 2.97, and an expected error near 1.07e-2, which agrees with the third marker close to the lower right corner of the panel. Read-off values carry a few percent uncertainty.

analyze.q: The lift moves from 0.093 to -0.012 between lc = 0.05 and 0.035. What does a sign change between two meshes imply about convergence, and what is the minimum number of further meshes you would add?
analyze.hint: Count the meshes you need for a trend.

analyze.q: The footnote on the image calls the pressure drop just below the interval at both mesh levels. Compare it with what the panel shows at lc = 0.05.
The pressure error order of 3.8 is higher than the velocity order of 3. List two reasons this could happen and what you would change to test each.
analyze.hint: Smooth manufactured pressure; coarse meshes outside the asymptotic range.

evaluate.q: The acceptance bar for the pressure order is above 1.5, while the measured order is 3.8. Is a bar that loose a good bar?
evaluate.hint: What failure would it still pass?

evaluate.q: The benchmark is labelled PASS for drag and FINDING for lift and pressure. Is a pass on one coefficient evidence that the setup matches the benchmark?
evaluate.hint: Which definitions are shared by all three coefficients.

create: Design the mesh sequence for the benchmark that would settle the lift coefficient: sizes, the number of meshes, and the plot that shows convergence into or away from the interval.
Redraw the manufactured-solution figure with mesh sizes n = 4, 6, 8 labelled, reference slopes of 2 and 3 drawn, no clipped markers and non-overlapping tick labels.

checks.q: Why is a drag value inside the published interval not proof that the solver has converged?
checks.hint: What is the interval the spread of?
checks.answer: The interval is the spread among established codes on fine meshes; it does not show your discretisation error is small, only that the value is consistent with theirs.

checks.q: Errors 0.025 and 0.0106 on meshes n = 6 and 8. What order?
Why can two mesh sizes not give a convergence order that you trust?
checks.answer: One slope has no check against curvature or the asymptotic range; a third mesh tests whether the slope is constant.

checks.q: The lift is -0.012 on the finest mesh and the reference is 0.008 to 0.01. What do you write?
checks.hint: Separate the observation from the claim.
checks.answer: Lift changes sign between two meshes and is not converged at these resolutions; no claim of agreement with the interval is made.

checks.q: How would you test that a pressure order of 3.8 is not an artefact of the coarse meshes?
checks.hint: Add meshes and vary the manufactured field.
checks.answer: Run at least two finer meshes and a second manufactured pressure with less smoothness; if the order falls toward the theoretical value, the first result was pre-asymptotic.

provenance.author: agent
provenance.notes: Disclosure: the images carry PASS and FINDING banners, a footnote on the benchmark figure referring to a region-indicator hypothesis (xy-only versus z-restricted) that was ruled out, and a footnote on the MMS figure that says 'Genuine new 3D derivation this session' and refers to an A.0 direct-LU cost-scaling finding. These session and milestone remarks are internal and are not repeated; the page teaches the generic reading. Owner review: (1) DFG figure x axis is labelled 'coarse to fine, right to left' but its tick labels run 0.0500 on the left to 0.0350 on the right, so fine is on the right as drawn. (2) The DFG footnote says the pressure drop 'sits just below [0.165, 0.175] at both levels', but the coarse point (0.166) lies inside the band and only the fine point (0.162) lies below it. (3) Only two meshes are shown, so the lift sign change cannot be called a trend. (4) In the MMS figure the third point is clipped by the panel frame and the x tick labels overlap. (5) Pressure order 3.8 exceeds the velocity order 3, and the bars (> 2.5, > 1.5) are looser than the measured values; the element pair is not stated. (6) The reference intervals come from a published benchmark named in the legend; no cite key for it exists in refs.js, so it is not cited by key.
